notes.b: Sedimentary rocks are laid down in layers called strata, or beds, formed by deposition followed by compaction and cementation.
points: A bedding plane is the boundary between one layer and the next; when laid down, bedding planes are roughly horizontal.
A bedding plane marks a pause or change in deposition.
Bedding planes divide the rock into layers, and each layer may differ in thickness and resistance.

notes.b: A joint is a crack in rock along which no movement has taken place.
points: Joints in sedimentary rock are at right angles to the bedding planes, so they are vertical where the strata are horizontal.
Joints form as sediment dries and shrinks, and by stress and the removal of overlying rock.
Dip is the angle at which strata tilt from the horizontal; the dip direction is the way they tilt.
Strike is the direction along a tilted layer's surface, at right angles to the dip.
Strata are horizontal, gently dipping or steeply dipping, and the landform depends on which.
Water, ice and weathering exploit bedding planes and joints as lines of weakness.
Rock breaks into blocks along these planes, so erosion is concentrated there.
Where resistant layers, such as sandstone and limestone, alternate with weak layers, such as shale and clay, the weak layers are worn away faster.
The resistant layers are left standing out as cliffs and caps.
Water passes down joints and bedding planes in permeable rock.
Water flows over impermeable rock instead.
A spring emerges where a permeable layer lies on an impermeable one, and the line of springs is a spring line.
1. Horizontal strata have a resistant cap rock lying above weaker layers.
2. Erosion strips the weaker layers beneath the cap and wears back the edges of the upland.
3. The cap protects the layers beneath, so the top stays flat and the edges stay steep.
Diagram: cross-section of a flat-topped upland with a resistant cap, cliffed edges and weaker strata below.
Alternating hard and soft horizontal layers erode at different rates.
Hard layers form cliffs; soft layers form gentler slopes, often covered by scree.
The profile of cliff and slope repeats for each pair of hard and soft layers.

notes.b: Near-horizontal Carboniferous strata of limestone, shale and sandstone form flat-topped uplands with steep cliffed edges and stepped slopes.
points: The Dartry Mountains and Cuilcagh span Co. Sligo, Co. Cavan and Co. Fermanagh.
Caves and karst features lie in the limestone beneath the uplands.
Benbulben, at 526 m, is a flat-topped mountain of near-horizontal strata.
A resistant limestone cap forms its vertical cliffs.
Weaker shale beneath forms the lower, gentler slopes, partly covered in scree.
Ice later steepened its sides.
Cuilcagh, at 665 m, is the highest point in both Co. Cavan and Co. Fermanagh.
A resistant sandstone cap lies over shale, which lies over limestone, giving a stepped profile and a flat summit ridge.
The Shannon Pot, the source of the River Shannon, lies at the foot of Cuilcagh in Co. Cavan.
The Marble Arch Caves, Co. Fermanagh, lie in the limestone beneath it.
1. Weathering and erosion work back the edges of a plateau.
2. The plateau is broken into separate flat-topped remnants, each capped by the resistant rock.
3. A mesa is wider than it is high; a butte is a smaller, narrower remnant.
Example: Monument Valley, on the Arizona–Utah border, USA.
Diagram: cross-section of a mesa and a butte, each with a resistant cap.
1. On gently dipping strata, a resistant layer is exposed at the surface.
2. Erosion cuts a steep scarp slope across the edges of the layers.
3. The layers continue along the tilt as a long, gentle dip slope.
4. The weaker rock between cuestas is eroded into a vale.
Example: the Cotswolds, England, a limestone cuesta with a steep west-facing scarp and a long dip slope to the east.
Diagram: cross-section of a cuesta showing scarp slope, dip slope and vale.
A hogback forms on steeply dipping strata.
It is a narrow ridge whose scarp and dip slopes are of nearly equal steepness.
Example: the Hog's Back, Surrey, England, a narrow chalk ridge.

notes.h: Bedding planes and joints in smaller landforms
points: Joints and bedding planes in limestone give limestone pavement, with blocks called clints separated by grikes.
Caves form along bedding planes in limestone.
Waterfalls form over horizontal cap rock.
Sea caves and arches form along joints on the coast.

notes.b: A saucer-shaped basin of sedimentary layers of different resistance, dipping gently in towards Paris.
points: The layers are limestone, chalk and clay.
Paris lies near the centre of the basin.
On the eastern side, resistant layers form outward-facing escarpments (cuestas), with dip slopes facing in towards Paris.
Gently dipping Old Red Sandstone forms flat-topped summits.
The summits have steep north-facing escarpments and gentle south-facing dip slopes.
Pen y Fan, at 886 m, is the highest peak in southern Britain.
The area was renamed Bannau Brycheiniog National Park in 2023.

keyTerms.definition: Layers of sedimentary rock, laid down by deposition and then compacted and cemented.
The boundary between one sedimentary layer and the next, roughly horizontal when the layers are laid down.
A crack in rock along which no movement has taken place, here at right angles to the bedding planes in sedimentary rock.
The angle at which strata tilt from the horizontal.
The direction along a tilted layer's surface, at right angles to the dip.
A bedding plane or joint along which water, ice and weathering break the rock.
Rock through which water can pass, down joints and bedding planes.
A line of springs where a permeable layer lies on an impermeable one.
The steep slope cut across the edges of tilted layers.
The gentle slope that follows the tilt of the layers.
An asymmetric ridge on gently dipping strata, with a steep scarp slope and a long dip slope.
A flat-topped hill with a resistant cap, wider than it is high.
A smaller, narrower flat-topped remnant with a resistant cap.
A narrow ridge on steeply dipping strata, with scarp and dip slopes of nearly equal steepness.
The blocks of limestone pavement (clints) separated by the cracks between them (grikes).

questions.prompt: Examine how sedimentary structures influence the development of landforms, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Bedding planes and joints are lines of weakness: water, ice and weathering exploit them, so rock breaks into blocks along them and erosion is concentrated there. Where resistant layers alternate with weak layers, the weak layers are worn away faster and the resistant layers stand out as cliffs and caps, a process of differential erosion. Where strata are horizontal, a resistant cap protects the layers beneath and the result is a plateau with a flat top and steep edges. Benbulben, Co. Sligo, at 526 m, is a flat-topped mountain of near-horizontal strata: a limestone cap forms vertical cliffs, and weaker shale beneath forms gentler slopes partly covered in scree. Cuilcagh, at 665 m, has a sandstone cap over shale over limestone, giving a stepped profile and a flat summit ridge. Monument Valley, USA, shows how the edges of a plateau retreat into mesas and buttes. Permeability controls water: water passes down joints and bedding planes in permeable rock and flows over impermeable rock, and springs emerge where permeable rock lies on impermeable rock. Where strata dip gently, the Paris Basin shows the result: resistant limestone and chalk form outward-facing cuestas with steep scarp slopes and gentle dip slopes, and clay vales lie between them. The Brecon Beacons in south Wales have gently dipping Old Red Sandstone, with steep north-facing escarpments and gentle south-facing dip slopes. Limestone areas also carry karst features, such as clints and grikes on pavements and caves along bedding planes.

questions.prompt: Explain, with the aid of a labelled diagram, how an escarpment (cuesta) forms.
questions.model: A cuesta forms on gently dipping strata where a resistant layer lies over weaker layers. Diagram: a labelled cross-section showing the dipping resistant layer, the weaker layer beneath it, the steep scarp slope, the long gentle dip slope following the tilt of the resistant layer, and the vale eroded in the weaker rock. Stage 1: the strata are tilted gently, so a resistant layer such as limestone or chalk lies over softer clay or shale. Stage 2: erosion removes the weaker rock beneath the resistant layer at the edge, cutting a steep scarp slope across the edges of the layers. Stage 3: the resistant layer continues along its tilt, forming a long, gentle dip slope on the other side. Stage 4: the weaker rock between two cuestas is eroded into a clay vale. Example: the Cotswolds, England, a limestone cuesta with a steep west-facing scarp and a long dip slope to the east. The Paris Basin has a series of cuestas with escarpments facing outwards and dip slopes facing in towards Paris.

questions.prompt: Explain the terms bedding plane and joint.
questions.model: A bedding plane is the boundary between one sedimentary layer and the next, roughly horizontal when the layers are laid down; it marks a pause or change in deposition. A joint is a crack in rock along which no movement has taken place; in sedimentary rock joints are at right angles to the bedding planes and form as sediment dries and shrinks, and by stress and the removal of overlying rock.
